meta.blurb: Lena is still studying at three in the morning, with an exam in two weeks. Her aunt Rosa, a sleep technician, shows her what the brain does at night and why sleep may beat one more late hour.
meta.bible: Lena: a university student of about twenty, with an exam in Two weeks, who stays up too late. Rosa: Lena's aunt, a sleep technician at a sleep clinic, patient and funny. They talk in Lena's small flat and on walks in the park. Key terms: Circadian, Melatonin, Adenosine, Caffeine, Glymphatic, REM, Insomnia, Apnoea, Cortisol, Dopamine, Microsleep, Chronotype, Larks, Owls, Dolphins. Real science only, hedged where research is uncertain: no invented numbers or studies; some findings come mostly from animals and the book says so. Voice: friendly, lively, clear, never scary. Nobody gets personal medical advice; the book gives general information and tells readers to see a doctor about their own health. This book is general information and is not medical advice. New names and facts for the full-length book: Kofi: Lena's classmate and friend, who studies for the same exam and drinks too many energy drinks; he joins the plan later. Mina: Rosa's colleague at the clinic, a proud owl who works the late shift. Biscuit: Lena's grey cat. The exam is in economics. Rosa works at a sleep clinic in the city. Day by day the book follows Lena's two weeks of trying Rosa's plan. More terms used: Suprachiasmatic, Hippocampus, Amygdala, Spindles, Orthosomnia, Polysomnography, Inertia, Cortisol, Cassiopea. Lena's grandmother lives nearby and sleeps lightly; Kofi's uncle sleeps badly and Kofi urges him to see a doctor; Kofi has felt low and Rosa says to see a doctor. Nobody in the book gives personal medical advice.
chapters: What Sleep Does for the Body

beats.scene: Lena studies at a desk at three in the morning beside a glowing phone
beats.summary: Lena is studying at three in the morning with an exam in two weeks.

beats.scene: A grey cat sleeps on open books beside cold cups of coffee
beats.summary: Her cat Biscuit sleeps on her notes while Lena counts six cold cups of coffee.

beats.scene: Two phones show late night messages between Lena and Kofi
beats.summary: Her classmate Kofi texts that he is awake too, and they joke about who sleeps least.

beats.scene: Lena rubs her eyes and reads the same line again and again
beats.summary: Lena reads one line three times and understands nothing, but still refuses to stop.

beats.scene: Aunt Rosa in a coat stands in Lena's doorway holding a bag of fruit
beats.summary: In the morning her aunt Rosa, who works at a sleep clinic, arrives with fruit.

beats.scene: Rosa looks at the desk of cups, papers and a dim lamp
beats.summary: Rosa sees the cups and the grey face and says sleep is the best study tool.

beats.scene: Lena and Rosa shake hands over a kitchen table with a calendar
beats.summary: Lena agrees to a two-week deal: try Rosa's plan and judge it by her exam.

beats.scene: A sleep diary notebook with columns for bedtime, wake time and coffee
beats.summary: Rosa asks Lena to keep a simple diary of bedtimes, wake times and coffee.

beats.scene: A clock face with one third filled by a sleeping figure
beats.summary: We spend about a third of life asleep, and it is not wasted time.

beats.scene: Animals asleep in nests, burrows and treetops under a night sky
beats.summary: Almost every animal studied sleeps despite the danger, so sleep must be vital.

beats.scene: A wall chart of sleeping figures from a tiny baby to an elderly person
beats.summary: Rosa shows a chart of how sleep needs change from birth to old age.

beats.scene: Four sleepers of different ages lie in beds from small to large
beats.summary: Babies sleep most of the day and school children need about nine to eleven hours.

beats.scene: A teenager and an adult asleep under blankets beside two clocks
beats.summary: Teenagers need about eight to ten hours and most adults need seven to nine.

beats.scene: Lena shrugs at a mug while Rosa raises one eyebrow
beats.summary: Lena says five hours feels fine, and Rosa says feeling fine and performing well are different.

beats.scene: A brain glows with moving coloured waves inside a sleeping head
beats.summary: Sleep is an active state in which the brain is busy and goes through stages.

beats.scene: A phone screen with a reaction game and a slow finger
beats.summary: Rosa gives Lena a quick reaction game, and Lena does worse than usual.

beats.scene: Two people in neighbouring beds, one tall and one small, both asleep
beats.summary: Sleep need is personal, partly in the genes, so two people can differ.

beats.scene: Two arrows labelled clock and pressure point at a sleeping moon
beats.summary: Rosa promises two forces decide when we sleep: a body clock and sleep pressure.

beats.scene: Lena and Rosa walk side by side along a park path under trees
beats.summary: They walk in the park, and Rosa says science comes first and rules second.

beats.scene: Lena sets a bedside alarm for one o'clock before bed
beats.summary: That night Lena goes to bed at one, two hours earlier than usual.

beats.scene: A sleep clinic room with a bed, wires and a screen of brain waves
beats.summary: Rosa describes her work: wires on the head and a screen showing sleeping brain waves.

beats.scene: A sleeper in a dim room with slow gentle waves drawn above the bed
beats.summary: Light sleep is the entry stage, easy to wake from, and the first minutes of the night.

beats.scene: A heart rate line slows beside a falling temperature line on a chart
beats.summary: In the next stage the heart slows, the body cools, and brief bursts of brain activity appear.

beats.scene: A sleeper lies very still while a slow thick wave rolls across a screen
beats.summary: Deep sleep brings slow, large brain waves and is hard to wake from.

beats.scene: A child asleep while small arrows show growth and repair in the body
beats.summary: In deep sleep the body repairs itself and releases growth hormone.

beats.scene: A sleeper's eyes move under closed lids while a dream cloud floats above
beats.summary: REM sleep brings vivid dreams, darting eyes and a brain almost as busy as when awake.

beats.scene: A sleeping figure with relaxed limbs while a dream of running floats above
beats.summary: In REM sleep the muscles are relaxed, so we do not act out our dreams.

beats.scene: A circular diagram of one night with four rounds of waves in a row
beats.summary: A night is made of cycles of about ninety minutes, four to six of them.

beats.scene: A night drawn as a chart with deep sleep early and dreaming sleep late
beats.summary: Deep sleep comes mostly early and REM sleep later, so short sleep cuts REM.

beats.scene: Lena draws a wavy night chart on a paper napkin at a cafe
beats.summary: Lena draws her own night on a napkin and learns that brief waking between cycles is normal.

beats.scene: A small clock glows inside a head beside a sun and a moon
beats.summary: The body clock runs on a rhythm of about twenty-four hours, set by a master clock in the brain.

beats.scene: A glowing dot behind two eyes with fine lines linking it to a clock
beats.summary: The master clock is a tiny cluster of cells behind the eyes.

beats.scene: A person in a cave with no windows beside a bed and a lamp
beats.summary: People who lived without clocks in caves still kept a daily rhythm close to twenty-four hours.

beats.scene: A day chart with temperature, alertness and hormones rising and falling in waves
beats.summary: The clock sets body temperature, hormones and alertness, not just sleep.

beats.scene: Morning sun shines through a window onto a sleepy face
beats.summary: Light, especially morning light, is the main signal that sets the body clock.

beats.scene: A close drawing of an eye with light rays reaching its back wall
beats.summary: Special cells in the eye measure brightness and tell the clock about the day.

beats.scene: A dark room with a small glowing moon and a calm sleeping figure
beats.summary: Melatonin rises in the evening when it gets dark and signals night to the body.

beats.scene: A bright ceiling lamp lights Lena's face at eleven at night
beats.summary: Rosa notices the bright lamp in Lena's flat at eleven and explains it fights melatonin.

beats.scene: A sunrise with a rising line labelled cortisol above a waking sleeper
beats.summary: In the morning a hormone called cortisol rises and helps us wake up.

beats.scene: Lena wraps a blanket around herself on a chilly sofa before dawn
beats.summary: Body temperature falls through the night, which is why four in the morning feels so cold.

beats.scene: A bird at sunrise and an owl at midnight look at a clock
beats.summary: Some people are larks and some are owls, partly because of genes.

beats.scene: Rosa and Lena in the park at dawn watching early runners
beats.summary: At dawn they meet early runners and cheerful larks who love the morning.

beats.scene: Mina in a clinic coat yawns happily at a night desk with a lamp
beats.summary: Rosa's colleague Mina is a proud owl who works the late shift.

beats.scene: A tired owl at a desk while a morning bus waits outside
beats.summary: Owls forced into early starts live in a kind of permanent jet lag.

beats.scene: Lena looks at a window with dawn colours over her phone-lit desk
beats.summary: Lena finds she is a mild owl, but three in the morning is extreme.

beats.scene: A group of teenagers asleep at desks in an early morning classroom
beats.summary: The teenage body clock shifts later, which makes early starts hard.

beats.scene: A bus full of drowsy teenagers pulling up to a school at dawn
beats.summary: Teenagers are not lazy; their clocks truly tell them it is still night.

beats.scene: A school clock showing a later start with students walking in smiling
beats.summary: Some schools that started later found that students slept more.

beats.scene: An older woman sits by a window at first light with a cup
beats.summary: With age the clock often moves earlier again, and older people wake earlier.

beats.scene: Lena sets two bedside lamps, one dim and one bright, on a shelf
beats.summary: Lena cannot change her type, but she can nudge her clock with light.

beats.scene: A tall tower of small blocks grows beside a clock
beats.summary: Sleep pressure builds the longer we are awake, linked to a chemical called adenosine.

beats.scene: A tower of blocks falls apart over a sleeping figure
beats.summary: Sleep clears adenosine away, so we wake with the pressure low.

beats.scene: A tired figure at four in the morning beside a bright window
beats.summary: In an all-nighter, the clock's morning push can give a false second wind.

beats.scene: A steaming coffee cup sits at four in the afternoon on a desk
beats.summary: Caffeine blocks adenosine's signal, so it hides tiredness instead of removing it.

beats.scene: A cup beside an hourglass whose sand runs slowly through
beats.summary: Caffeine stays in the body for hours, with half still there after about five.

beats.scene: Lena counts six cups lined up on a kitchen counter
beats.summary: Lena counts her cups in the diary and finds the last one is at nine at night.

beats.scene: A coffee cup drawn beside a bed and a clock reading six hours
beats.summary: One well-known experiment found coffee six hours before bed still cut sleep.

beats.scene: A figure yawns at a desk while a clock reads two
beats.summary: There is a natural dip in alertness in the early afternoon.

beats.scene: A person naps on a sofa under a blanket beside a clock
beats.summary: A short nap can help, but long naps late in the day can spoil night sleep.

beats.scene: Lena naps under a blanket with Biscuit asleep on her feet
beats.summary: Lena tries a twenty-minute nap with Biscuit and wakes fresh for the first time in weeks.

beats.scene: A brain turns the pages of a glowing book while a figure sleeps below
beats.summary: Sleep helps the brain to store and organise what has been learned.

beats.scene: A small inbox tray beside a tall library of shelves, connected by arrows
beats.summary: Rosa compares the brain's short-term store to an inbox and long-term memory to a library.

beats.scene: Brain waves with small bursts marked above a sleeping head
beats.summary: During sleep the brain replays the day, and brief bursts of activity seem to help.

beats.scene: Old black and white students in beds and at desks with word lists
beats.summary: An old experiment in 1924 found students remembered more after sleep than after hours awake.

beats.scene: A child falls asleep over a storybook beside a lamp
beats.summary: Studies in many ages find sleep after learning improves recall, from children to adults.

beats.scene: A sponge labelled tired brain refusing to soak up water
beats.summary: After a sleepless night the brain is also worse at taking in new facts.

beats.scene: Lena and Kofi plan a study timetable on a whiteboard with moons
beats.summary: Lena closes her books at night while a dim moon shines through the window.

beats.scene: Fingers tapping a keyboard in a pattern beside a sleeping moon
beats.summary: Skills such as typing or piano also improve after sleep.

beats.scene: A figure wakes with a lit bulb above beside a puzzle
beats.summary: In some studies, people were likelier to spot a hidden shortcut after sleep.

beats.scene: Lena smiles at a practice exam question with a formula she remembers
beats.summary: A few nights later Lena finds she recalls a formula that she once forgot.

beats.scene: A gentle stream of blue light runs through a brain while a figure sleeps
beats.summary: The brain may clear waste during sleep, shown mainly in animals so far.

beats.scene: A mouse brain drawn with wider channels and flowing liquid
beats.summary: In mice, the spaces between brain cells widened during sleep and fluid flowed through them.

beats.scene: A scientist's notebook with a question mark beside a human head
beats.summary: In people the evidence is still growing, and scientists do not yet know the full story.

beats.scene: A tired head with a small marker labelled protein beside a bed
beats.summary: Early research hints at links between poor sleep and memory trouble later in life.

beats.scene: Lena frowns at an annoying message on her phone with tired eyes
beats.summary: Poor sleep makes emotions stronger and people more irritable.

beats.scene: A brain scan with a small alarm bell glowing brighter than usual
beats.summary: Brain scans suggest the emotional alarm centre reacts more after short sleep.

beats.scene: A dreamer holds a heavy memory that slowly fades into soft light
beats.summary: REM sleep may help to soften the sting of emotional memories, though it is not proven.

beats.scene: Two arrows loop between a sleeping moon and a thoughtful face
beats.summary: Sleep and mental health affect each other.

beats.scene: Rosa speaks gently to Lena with a phone showing a doctor's number
beats.summary: Low mood that lasts is a reason to see a doctor, and Rosa says she is not one.

beats.scene: Kofi laughs with Lena over lunch in a sunny cafe
beats.summary: After a good night Lena laughs more easily and Kofi notices.

beats.scene: A tissue box and a mug beside a person with a cold
beats.summary: Kofi sneezes through a cold and Rosa says sleep helps the body's defences.

beats.scene: Volunteers with cold viruses in clean rooms drawn as small figures in beds
beats.summary: One study found that people who slept less were more likely to catch a cold.

beats.scene: A syringe and a small calendar beside a sleeping figure
beats.summary: Some studies suggest sleep helps the body respond better to vaccines.

beats.scene: A heart drawn on a night chart dips gently as a sleeper rests
beats.summary: At night blood pressure usually falls, giving the heart a rest.

beats.scene: A heart beside a long row of dark nights drawn on a calendar
beats.summary: Long-term short sleep is linked with heart problems, but a link is not proof.

beats.scene: A person at a fridge in the night light with a plate of biscuits
beats.summary: Lena finds she eats biscuits at two in the morning and wonders why.

beats.scene: Two hormone bottles labelled hungry and full tilting in different directions
beats.summary: Short sleep seems to raise hunger hormones and lower fullness ones.

beats.scene: A person with an aching back lies awake counting the minutes
beats.summary: In some studies, poor sleep makes pain feel worse.

beats.scene: A runner in a park resting on grass beside a water bottle
beats.summary: After hard exercise, sleep helps muscles recover, and athletes often value it.

beats.scene: Rosa taps a drawing of a house resting on a solid base
beats.summary: Rosa says sleep is a foundation, not a cure-all, and health worries need a doctor.

beats.scene: A car on a dark road, the driver's eyes closing
beats.summary: Drowsy driving is dangerous and causes many accidents.

beats.scene: A road sign beside a motorway at night with a rest stop
beats.summary: Rosa says many clinic patients first come after a near miss on the road.

beats.scene: A glass of wine sits next to a clock showing a long night awake
beats.summary: Being awake for about seventeen hours can affect performance like a small amount of alcohol.

beats.scene: A student's head drops at a lecture desk for a moment while others write
beats.summary: Microsleeps are short moments of sleep that happen without warning.

beats.scene: Lena in a lecture hall with a pen sliding off her page
beats.summary: In a lecture Lena has a microsleep and misses a whole minute.

beats.scene: A driver yawns while a roadside sign shows a rest area
beats.summary: The warning signs are yawning, heavy eyes and missing turns; pull over safely.

beats.scene: A person with a coffee mug proudly holds up five fingers
beats.summary: Most people who say they cope on five hours still perform worse.

beats.scene: A smiling family of three beside a tiny gene symbol
beats.summary: A few rare families carry a gene change that lets them sleep less.

beats.scene: A phone reaction game showing a better score beside a rested face
beats.summary: After a good night Lena repeats the reaction game and does clearly better.

beats.scene: Kofi holds a clean notebook headed with a new plan for sleep
beats.summary: Kofi decides to join the plan too.

beats.scene: A bank statement with hours instead of coins showing a debt
beats.summary: Lost sleep adds up like a debt that grows each night.

beats.scene: A calendar with a weekend circled and a sleeper lying late in bed
beats.summary: Sleep debt can be partly paid back, but weekend lie-ins do not fully repair the damage.

beats.scene: A Monday morning clock and a tired figure pulling on a sweater
beats.summary: Sleeping very late at weekends can shift the body clock and make Monday harder.

beats.scene: A row of earlier bedtime moons on a calendar over several nights
beats.summary: The kindest way to repay a debt is a few earlier nights in a row.

beats.scene: A cat, a bat, an elephant and a giraffe, each asleep differently
beats.summary: Animals sleep very differently, from cats and bats that sleep long to elephants that sleep short.

beats.scene: A dolphin glides through blue water with one eye open and one eye closed
beats.summary: Dolphins sleep with half the brain at a time.

beats.scene: A duck at the end of a row of ducks with one eye open
beats.summary: Some birds and seals also sleep with half the brain, watching for danger.

beats.scene: Lena sits up in bed in a dream-twisted room full of exam papers
beats.summary: Lena has a strange dream about her exam and tells Rosa about it.

beats.scene: A dreamer floats above a bed among soft clouds and strange shapes
beats.summary: Scientists do not fully know why we dream, though dreams may help memory and emotion.

beats.scene: A notebook beside a bed with a half-written dream note
beats.summary: Everyone dreams, most dreams are forgotten, and nightmares are common and usually normal.

beats.scene: Lena looks around her cluttered bedroom with a desk, lights and cables
beats.summary: Rosa walks through Lena's bedroom and finds a desk, bright lights and a lot of cables.

beats.scene: Lena arranges dark curtains over a window beside a sleep mask
beats.summary: A dark room helps sleep, and thick curtains or a mask can make the difference.

beats.scene: A pair of earplugs and a small fan on a bedside table
beats.summary: Quiet helps too, and earplugs or steady sounds can cover street noise.

beats.scene: A thermometer on a bedroom wall beside an open window at night
beats.summary: A slightly cool bedroom helps the body's temperature drop, which helps sleep.

beats.scene: A desk moves out of a bedroom into a corner of the living room
beats.summary: Lena moves her desk out so that the bed is only for sleep.

beats.scene: A bed with a soft pillow and a blanket in warm lamplight
beats.summary: There is no magic mattress; a bed that feels comfortable is the right one.

beats.scene: A bedside clock turned to face the wall
beats.summary: A clock turned to the wall stops the worry of watching the minutes.

beats.scene: Lena in a warm bath with steam and a book
beats.summary: A warm bath an hour or two before bed can help, because the body cools afterwards.

beats.scene: Lena lies in the changed bedroom looking at the dark ceiling
beats.summary: The first night in the new bedroom feels strange to Lena.

beats.scene: Lena wakes in soft light and stretches in her calm room
beats.summary: Rosa says benefits take days to show, and Lena sees small signs.

beats.scene: A glowing phone screen shines in the dark beside a dim yellow lamp
beats.summary: Bright light in the evening can delay sleepiness; dim, warm light is better.

beats.scene: Lena scrolls her phone under a blanket with a blue glow on her face
beats.summary: Lena scrolls in bed until one and wonders why she is not sleepy.

beats.scene: A tablet and a paper book each beside a small glowing moon
beats.summary: A study found reading on a light-emitting screen delayed melatonin compared with paper.

beats.scene: A stream of endless video clips leaving a phone screen
beats.summary: It is not only light: endless videos and messages keep the mind alert.

beats.scene: Lena swaps a bright white bulb for a soft yellow one
beats.summary: Lena replaces her bright bulb with a dim, warm one.

beats.scene: A phone with a yellow night mode icon beside a small moon
beats.summary: Night mode helps a little, but putting the phone away works better.

beats.scene: A phone charging on a kitchen counter, far from a bedroom door
beats.summary: Lena charges her phone in the kitchen overnight.

beats.scene: Kofi and Lena hold phones with a do not disturb moon icon
beats.summary: Kofi worries about midnight messages, so they agree to use silent mode.

beats.scene: A cheap round alarm clock sits on a bedside table
beats.summary: Lena buys a plain alarm clock so the phone need not wake her.

beats.scene: Lena reads a paperback by a small lamp with Biscuit curled up
beats.summary: The first phone-free hour is boring, then Lena enjoys a paper novel.

beats.scene: A calendar shows the same wake time written on each morning
beats.summary: A regular wake-up time helps the body clock, even at weekends.

beats.scene: A calendar with a small band around the wake time on every day
beats.summary: Rosa suggests keeping the wake time within about an hour every day.

beats.scene: Lena stands on a balcony in bright morning light with a cup of tea
beats.summary: Bright morning light and being outdoors help to set the body clock.

beats.scene: A cloudy sky above a street with a bright sun symbol and a window
beats.summary: Even a cloudy day outside is many times brighter than a lit room.

beats.scene: A finger hovers over a snooze button on a ringing alarm
beats.summary: Snoozing mostly gives broken, shallow sleep, so Lena sets one alarm.

beats.scene: A groggy sleeper sits on the bed edge with eyes half shut
beats.summary: Grogginess in the first minutes after waking is normal and is called sleep inertia.

beats.scene: A glass of water, an open window and a stretching figure at dawn
beats.summary: Water, light and a few stretches help Lena wake up gently.

beats.scene: A clock showing two in the afternoon beside an empty coffee cup
beats.summary: Many experts suggest limiting caffeine in the afternoon and evening.

beats.scene: Cups of tea, cola and a chocolate bar on a table
beats.summary: Caffeine hides in tea, cola and chocolate, not only in coffee.

beats.scene: Lena pours herbal tea and takes a walk instead of a late coffee
beats.summary: Lena swaps her afternoon coffee for water and a short walk.

beats.scene: A birthday cake with candles and friends holding glasses in a crowded flat
beats.summary: At Kofi's birthday party Lena is offered a glass of wine.

beats.scene: A glass of wine on a bedside table next to a restless sleeper
beats.summary: Alcohol can make you drowsy but it breaks up sleep and reduces REM.

beats.scene: A chart of a night with alcohol and a broken second half
beats.summary: The second half of a night after alcohol is lighter and more broken.

beats.scene: A late dinner table with big plates and a clock reading eleven
beats.summary: A big, heavy meal close to bedtime can disturb sleep, though a light snack is fine.

beats.scene: A mug of warm milk beside a cosy blanket and slippers
beats.summary: Warm milk may work mostly as a comforting habit, with little strong evidence.

beats.scene: Lena in running shoes jogs through a park in the late afternoon sun
beats.summary: Regular physical activity tends to improve sleep; time of day matters little for most people.

beats.scene: Rosa and Lena run side by side through a park in golden light
beats.summary: Lena runs with Rosa in the late afternoon and enjoys it.

beats.scene: A runner stopping to rest at sunset with a bedtime clock beside
beats.summary: Very hard exercise close to bedtime may keep some people awake, so listen to your body.

beats.scene: A runner outdoors in bright morning light with trees overhead
beats.summary: Exercise outdoors in daylight gives two benefits at once.

beats.scene: Lena tucked in bed, eyes closing as the clock reads half past ten
beats.summary: Lena notices she is falling asleep faster.

beats.scene: Rosa stands at a kitchen table with a cup beside an open diary
beats.summary: Rosa says sleep cannot be forced, only invited.

beats.scene: A series of small drawings: brushing teeth, dimming lights, closing curtains
beats.summary: A calm routine repeated each night teaches the body when sleep is coming.

beats.scene: A small notebook and a pen beside a lamp before bed
beats.summary: A small study found that writing a to-do list before bed helped people fall asleep faster.

beats.scene: Lena writes a list of exam topics in a notebook by a small lamp
beats.summary: Lena writes down tomorrow's tasks and her worries before bed.

beats.scene: A person lying back with a hand on their stomach, slow breathing
beats.summary: Slow breathing and muscle relaxation can calm the body for sleep.

beats.scene: Lena stands in a steamy shower with soft light
beats.summary: A warm shower can be part of the wind-down.

beats.scene: Lena lies awake with her face turned from a clock
beats.summary: If you cannot sleep, do not watch the clock.

beats.scene: Lena sits in a dim living room with a book at two
beats.summary: If awake for a long while, get up and do something calm instead of lying awake.

beats.scene: Lena puts the book down and walks back to bed with a yawn
beats.summary: Lena goes back to bed when sleepy and drops off.

beats.scene: Rosa and Lena share a smile over cups in a quiet kitchen
beats.summary: Rosa says do not turn sleep into a performance, because pressure makes it worse.

beats.scene: Rosa speaks gently to Lena at a kitchen table with a calendar
beats.summary: Insomnia is common, and many people have short spells of it.

beats.scene: A calendar with three nights each week marked for several months
beats.summary: Chronic insomnia means trouble sleeping at least three nights a week for about three months.

beats.scene: A tangle of strings labelled stress, pain, noise and habits
beats.summary: Insomnia has many causes, and not all of them are worry.

beats.scene: A person and a therapist sit in two chairs with a notebook
beats.summary: Talking therapy for insomnia is often recommended as the first treatment.

beats.scene: A notebook with a bedtime schedule drawn beside a clock
beats.summary: This therapy teaches new sleep habits and calmer thoughts about sleep.

beats.scene: A pill bottle on a shelf behind a closed cabinet door
beats.summary: Sleeping tablets are usually for short use and are not the first long-term answer.

beats.scene: Kofi on the phone about a relative who cannot sleep
beats.summary: Kofi worries about a relative who has not slept well for months.

beats.scene: A doctor's desk with a calendar and a notepad
beats.summary: If poor sleep lasts for weeks, or troubles daytime life, see a doctor.

beats.scene: Lena looks out a window thoughtfully with the morning light on her face
beats.summary: Lena understands that sleeplessness is not weakness or laziness.

beats.scene: A road lit by street lamps leading toward a lit clinic window
beats.summary: Rosa invites Lena to see the clinic at work one evening.

beats.scene: Lena walks into a quiet clinic corridor with doors like hotel rooms
beats.summary: Lena visits Rosa's clinic, where the rooms look like small hotel rooms.

beats.scene: Mina attaches small sensors to a model head in a dim room
beats.summary: Mina shows the sensors that record brain waves, eyes, muscles and heart.

beats.scene: A chest belt, a finger clip and a small nose tube on a table
beats.summary: Other sensors measure breathing and the oxygen in the blood.

beats.scene: A sleeper with a mask on a pillow and a sound wave above
beats.summary: Sleep apnoea is when breathing stops or narrows during sleep.

beats.scene: A throat drawn narrow beside a brain that wakes with a spark
beats.summary: In apnoea the throat narrows and the brain briefly wakes to restart breathing.

beats.scene: A loud snoring figure beside a tired face with a headache
beats.summary: Loud snoring, gasping and tiredness mean you should see a doctor.

beats.scene: A sleeper in a lab bed watched through a window by a quiet technician
beats.summary: People do not always know they have it, and a sleep study can find out.

beats.scene: A doctor explains a small mask connected to a quiet machine
beats.summary: Treatments exist, and a doctor chooses which fits each person.

beats.scene: Mina points to a calm trace with clear cycles on a screen
beats.summary: Lena recognises the cycles she learned on a calm sleeper's screen.

beats.scene: Lena walks home along a quiet street as dawn begins to colour the sky
beats.summary: Lena walks home at dawn, thinking about all the hidden work of sleep.

A1A2: It is three in the morning, and Lena is still studying hard.
Her cat Biscuit sleeps on the notes, next to six cold cups.
Her friend Kofi sends a message and says he is awake too.
Lena reads one line three times, but she understands nothing at all.
In the morning, her aunt Rosa arrives with a bag of fruit.
Rosa works at a sleep clinic, and she sees Lena's grey, tired face.
Lena agrees to try Rosa's plan for two weeks, and then she will decide.
Rosa gives Lena a notebook to write down when she sleeps and wakes.
People spend about one third of their lives asleep.
Nearly every animal sleeps, so sleep must be very important for life.
Rosa draws a chart to show how much sleep people need at each age.
Babies sleep for most of the day, and school children need about ten hours.
Teenagers need about nine hours, and most adults need seven to nine.
Lena says five hours is fine, but Rosa is not so sure.
Sleep is not like turning off a light, because the brain stays busy.
Rosa gives Lena a quick phone game, and Lena plays badly.
Some people need a little more sleep, and some need a little less.
Rosa says two things decide when we sleep: the body clock and feeling tired.
They walk in the park, and Rosa says facts come before rules.
That night, Lena goes to bed at one, not at three.
Rosa works with wires and screens that show how people sleep.
Light sleep comes first, and you wake up easily from it.
Then the heart goes slower, and the body gets a little cooler.
In deep sleep, the brain makes slow, big waves, and waking is hard.
In deep sleep the body repairs itself and helps children to grow.
In REM sleep, the eyes move fast and the dreams feel very real.
In REM sleep the muscles rest, so people do not act out dreams.
One night has four to six cycles, and each cycle lasts about ninety minutes.
Deep sleep comes early in the night, and REM sleep comes later.
Lena draws her night on paper, and Rosa says waking sometimes is normal.
The body has a clock that runs on a day of about twenty-four hours.
The master clock is a tiny group of cells behind the eyes.
People who lived in caves without clocks still kept a daily rhythm.
The clock changes body heat and how awake we feel during the day.
Morning light tells the clock that the day has begun.
Special cells in the eye feel the light and tell the clock.
In the evening, when it gets dark, the body makes more melatonin.
Rosa sees Lena's bright lamp at eleven and says it fights melatonin.
In the morning, the body makes cortisol, and it helps you wake up.
At night the body gets cooler, so four in the morning feels cold.
At dawn, Rosa and Lena see men and women running in the park.
Some people are larks who love mornings, and some are owls who stay up late.
Rosa's friend Mina is an owl, and she likes to work at night.
An owl with an early job can feel tired all the time.
Lena is a little bit of an owl, but three is too late.
Teenagers have a body clock that moves later, so they get sleepy late.
A sleepy teenager is not lazy, because the body clock says it is night.
Some schools start later, and the students there sleep more.
Older people often get sleepy early and wake up early too.
Lena cannot change her type, but light can move her clock a little.
Adenosine is a chemical that builds up in the brain while you are awake.
Sleep clears away the adenosine, so you wake up feeling fresh.
After a night without sleep, you may feel a bit better at sunrise.
Caffeine does not take away the tired feeling, but it hides it.
Half of the caffeine is still in your body five hours later.
Lena counts six cups of coffee, and the last one was at nine.
A test showed that coffee six hours before bed made sleep shorter.
Many people feel sleepy in the early afternoon, and this is normal.
A short nap can help, but a long nap late in the day does not.
Lena takes a nap for twenty minutes and wakes up feeling fresh.
Sleep helps the brain to keep and sort what you learned.
Rosa says the brain has a small inbox and a big library.
At night, the brain goes over the day and moves facts to the library.
In 1924, students who slept remembered more than students who stayed awake.
Studies show that sleep after learning helps people of many ages.
After a night without sleep, the brain learns new things badly.
Lena and Kofi make a plan: study first, and then sleep.
Sleep also helps skills, like typing and playing the piano.
After sleep, people can find a clever shortcut to a hard puzzle.
A few nights later, Lena remembers a formula that she forgot.
The brain makes waste while it works, and it uses a lot of energy.
In mice, the brain seems to wash itself clean during sleep.
We know less about people, and scientists are still learning.
Some early studies link poor sleep with memory problems later in life.
Lena is angry at a silly message, because she slept badly.
Brain pictures show that the feeling centre is stronger after poor sleep.
Dream sleep may help to make sad memories feel softer.
Sleep and mood affect each other in both directions.
If a low mood lasts, a person should talk to a doctor.
After a good night, Lena laughs more, and Kofi sees it.
Kofi has a cold, and Rosa says sleep helps the body fight germs.
One study found that people who slept less caught more colds.
Some studies say that sleep helps the body respond to vaccines.
At night, blood pressure usually goes down, and the heart can rest.
People who sleep too little for years have more heart problems.
At two in the morning, Lena eats biscuits and wonders why.
Short sleep seems to make people feel more hungry in experiments.
In some studies, people with poor sleep feel more pain.
After hard exercise, sleep helps the muscles to recover and grow strong.
Rosa says sleep is a base for health, but it is not magic.
Driving when you are very tired is dangerous, and it causes many accidents.
Rosa says many of her patients first come after a near accident.
After about seventeen hours awake, the brain works as if you drank a little wine.
A microsleep is a very short sleep that comes without any warning.
In a lecture, Lena has a microsleep and misses one whole minute.
Heavy eyes and missing a turn are warning signs, so stop safely.
Many people say they are fine on five hours, but their tests are worse.
A few rare families have a gene that lets them sleep less.
After a good night, Lena plays the phone game again and does better.
Kofi decides to join the plan too.
Missed sleep is like a loan, and every short night adds to it.
A long sleep on Saturday pays back some of it, but not all.
Sleeping very late at weekends can make Monday morning harder.
A better way is to go to bed a bit earlier for a few days.
Cats and bats sleep for many hours, but elephants sleep only a few.
A dolphin sleeps with half of its brain at a time.
Some birds and seals can also sleep with one half of the brain.
Lena has a strange dream about her exam and tells Rosa.
No one knows exactly why we dream, but dreams may help memory.
Everyone dreams, but we forget most dreams, and bad dreams are normal.
Rosa looks at Lena's bedroom and sees a desk, bright lights and cables.
A dark room helps sleep, so Lena buys thick curtains and a mask.
A quiet room helps too, so Lena shuts out the noise of the street.
A room that is a little cool helps the body to sleep.
Lena moves her desk out, so the bed is only for sleep.
There is no magic bed, and a comfortable bed is the best one.
Lena turns her clock to the wall, so she cannot watch the time.
A warm bath one or two hours before bed can help sleep.
The first night in the new bedroom feels strange to Lena.
After a few days, Lena sees small signs that it is working.
Bright light in the evening can make you feel sleepy later.
In bed, Lena looks at her phone until two and does not feel sleepy.
A study found that a bright screen delays the night signal more than paper.
Videos and messages also keep the mind busy and awake.
Lena changes her bright white bulb for a soft, yellow one.
Night mode helps a little, but putting the phone away works better.
Now Lena charges her phone in the kitchen all night.
Kofi worries about late messages, so they use silent mode.
Lena buys a plain alarm clock, so the phone can sleep.
The first hour without a phone is boring, and then Lena enjoys a book.
A regular wake-up time helps the body clock, even at weekends.
Rosa says to wake up within one hour of the same time each day.
Lena stands on the balcony with a cup of tea in the morning light.
Even on a cloudy day, it is much brighter outside than inside.
Sleeping again after the alarm gives broken sleep, so Lena sets one alarm.
Feeling heavy for a few minutes after waking up is normal.
A glass of water, some light and a stretch help Lena wake up.
Many experts say to have less caffeine in the afternoon and evening.
Tea, cola and chocolate also have caffeine, not only coffee.
Lena has water and a short walk instead of an afternoon coffee.
At Kofi's birthday party, someone gives Lena a glass of wine.
Alcohol makes you sleepy, but it breaks up your sleep and cuts REM.
After alcohol, the second half of the night is light and broken.
A big, heavy meal just before bed can make sleep worse.
Warm milk may help only because it feels like a nice habit.
Regular exercise usually helps sleep, and the time of day matters little.
Lena runs with Rosa in the park in the late afternoon.
Very hard exercise just before bed may keep some people awake.
Exercise outside in daylight gives two good things at once.
Lena notices that she is falling asleep faster now.
Rosa says you cannot force sleep, but you can invite it.
A calm routine every night teaches the body that sleep is coming.
In a small study, writing a to-do list helped people fall asleep faster.
Lena writes down tomorrow's jobs and her worries before bed.
Slow breathing can calm the body and make it ready for sleep.
A warm shower can be part of the evening routine.
If you cannot sleep, do not watch the clock.
If you are awake for a long time, get up and do something calm.
Lena goes back to bed when she feels sleepy, and she falls asleep.
Rosa says sleep is not a test, because worry makes it harder.
Insomnia means trouble sleeping, and it is common.
Long-term insomnia means poor sleep three nights a week for three months.
Insomnia has many causes, and worry is only one of them.
Many experts say that talking therapy is the first treatment for it.
This therapy teaches new sleep habits and calmer thoughts about sleep.
Sleeping pills are for short use, and they are not the first answer.
Kofi's uncle has not slept well for months, and Kofi is worried.
If poor sleep lasts for weeks, a doctor can help.
Lena understands that poor sleep does not mean a person is weak or lazy.
Rosa asks Lena to visit the clinic one evening.
Lena visits the clinic, and the rooms look like small hotel rooms.
Mina shows how small sensors record brain waves, eyes, muscles and the heart.
Other sensors measure breathing and the oxygen in the blood.
Sleep apnoea means that breathing stops or gets narrow during sleep.
In apnoea, the throat gets narrow, and the brain wakes for a second.
Loud snoring, gasping and feeling tired all day are reasons to see a doctor.
People often do not know it, but a sleep study can find out.
There are treatments, and a doctor decides which one is right.
On a screen, Lena sees the cycles she learned about.
Lena walks home at dawn and thinks about the work of sleep.
Kofi has a small band on his arm that gives him a sleep score.
A tracker guesses your sleep from movement and heartbeat, so it is only rough.
Too much worry about scores is not good, so Lena uses them lightly.
Sleeping pills and other products should be discussed with a doctor.
Melatonin rules are different in each country, so ask a pharmacist.
When you fly far, your body clock stays behind, and light helps.
Night shift work is hard on the body clock, so sleep timing matters.
New babies sleep in short pieces, so tired parents are normal.
Older people often sleep more lightly, but they still need sleep.
Rosa, Lena and Kofi test five sleep myths, and all five are wrong.
The night before the exam, Lena closes her books at ten.
Lena follows her routine and sleeps well, with Biscuit on her feet.
She wakes up before her alarm, feeling rested and ready.
On the balcony, Lena has tea in the morning light and a small breakfast.
Kofi follows the plan too, and he walks with Lena and feels calm.
In the exam hall, Lena feels awake and not afraid.

After the exam, Lena walks into the sun, tired but happy.

B1B2: Lena has an exam in two weeks, and she has been studying until three every night. She is tired, but she believes that sleeping less will give her more time to learn.

Biscuit the cat has fallen asleep on Lena's notes, which is probably the best idea anyone has had tonight. Beside the keyboard stand six cold cups of coffee, and Lena cannot remember drinking half of them.
At ten past three her phone buzzes with a message from her classmate Kofi, who is awake as well. They joke about who has slept the least, and both of them are secretly proud of the answer.
Lena reads the same line of her textbook three times and still cannot say what it means. Her eyes burn, but she tells herself that one more hour will fix everything.
At eight in the morning there is a knock at the door, and her aunt Rosa walks in with a bag of fruit. She works at a sleep clinic, and she has come to see why Lena has not answered her calls.
Rosa looks at the cups, the papers and Lena's grey face, and she shakes her head kindly. She says that sleep is the best study tool Lena owns, and that Lena is not using it.
Lena is too tired to argue, so she makes a deal with her aunt. For two weeks she will try Rosa's plan, and then she will judge it by how her exam goes.
Rosa hands her a small notebook and asks her to keep a simple sleep diary. Every day Lena must write down when she goes to bed, when she wakes and when she drinks coffee.
Rosa begins with a simple fact about a whole life. If you live to be ninety, you will spend about thirty years asleep, and none of that time is wasted.
Rosa adds that nearly every animal scientists have studied sleeps, from fruit flies to whales. Sleeping leaves a creature helpless, so it must give something very valuable in return.
Rosa takes a pen and draws a chart that runs from a newborn baby to a very old person. It shows that the amount of sleep we need changes a lot during a lifetime.
Newborn babies sleep for most of the day and night, waking only to eat. School children need much more sleep than adults, usually about nine to eleven hours.
Teenagers do best with about eight to ten hours, although many of them get far less. Most adults need between seven and nine hours, and older adults still need about seven or eight.
Lena says that five hours feels perfectly fine to her. Rosa answers that feeling fine and working well are two different things, and she promises to prove it.
Many people think that sleep is like switching off a machine. In fact the brain stays very busy all night, and it moves through different stages, each with its own job.
Rosa opens a simple reaction game on her phone and asks Lena to tap the screen as fast as she can. Lena, who has not slept, taps late again and again, and her score is lower than she expected.
Rosa explains that the need for sleep is personal, and that genes play a part. Two people of the same age can need quite different amounts, so there is no single perfect number.
Rosa promises that two main forces decide when we sleep and when we wake. One is the body clock, and the other is a kind of pressure that builds while we stay awake.

They walk through the park, where the trees are beginning to turn yellow. Rosa tells Lena that the science comes first and the rules come second, because rules are easier to follow when you understand them.
That evening Lena does something new: she closes her laptop at midnight and gets into bed at one. It is only two hours earlier than usual, but her body seems surprised.
Rosa tells Lena what her job is really like on an ordinary night. At the clinic she puts small wires on a sleeping person's head, and a screen shows the brain waves rolling past all night.
Sleep starts with a very light stage that lasts only a few minutes. You can be woken so easily from it that many people later insist they were never asleep.

Next comes a slightly deeper stage, in which the heartbeat slows and the body cools a little. This stage fills about half of the whole night, and it includes brief bursts of brain activity that scientists call spindles.
After that comes deep sleep, when the brain makes slow, large waves. It is very hard to wake someone from it, and a person woken then may feel confused for several minutes.
Deep sleep is when the body does much of its repair work. It also releases growth hormone, which matters most for children and teenagers but still helps adults.
REM sleep is the stage in which most of our vivid dreams happen. Under the closed eyelids the eyes dart about, and the brain is almost as busy as it is when we are awake.
During REM sleep most of the body's muscles are almost switched off, so the body stays still. This is lucky, because otherwise we would act out our dreams and perhaps hurt ourselves.
The stages do not happen only once in a night, because they repeat in a loop. A full cycle lasts about ninety minutes, so a good night holds roughly four to six of them.
Deep sleep is concentrated in the first half of the night, while REM sleep grows longer toward morning. This means that if you cut your night short, you lose much of your REM sleep.
Lena draws a wavy chart of her own night on a paper napkin. Rosa tells her that short wakings between cycles are normal, and that most people forget them by morning.
Rosa explains that every person has a body clock that runs on a rhythm of about twenty-four hours. It is set by a master clock deep inside the brain, and it tells the body whether it is day or night.
The master clock is not large; it is a tiny cluster of cells that sits just behind the eyes. Scientists call it the suprachiasmatic nucleus, although most people simply say the body clock.

Years ago, some brave volunteers lived in caves with no clocks and no daylight for weeks. They still slept and woke in a steady daily rhythm, close to twenty-four hours, which shows that the clock lives inside us.
The clock does much more than tell us when to sleep. It also guides our body temperature, our hormones and how alert we feel at different times of the day.
The clock is not perfect, so it needs to be reset every day, and its main reset button is light. Morning light is especially powerful, because it tells the brain that a new day has really begun.
The eyes do more than let us see, because they also measure how bright the world is. Special cells at the back of each eye send that message straight to the master clock.

As evening comes and the light fades, the brain starts to release a hormone called melatonin. It does not knock you out, but it tells the body that night has begun and that sleep will soon be welcome.

One evening, around eleven, Rosa notices the bright white lamp on Lena's ceiling, and she raises an eyebrow. Strong light in the late evening tells the brain that it is still daytime, and so it delays the melatonin.
As morning approaches, the clock tells the body to release more of a hormone called cortisol. Cortisol helps to raise our energy and alertness, so it helps us to wake up and get moving.
Body temperature does not stay the same all through the day and night. It falls through the evening and reaches its lowest point in the early morning, so four o'clock often feels cold and lonely.
At six the next morning Rosa drags Lena to the park to watch the sunrise. Early runners go past in bright jackets, and some of them are smiling as if the day had been invented for them.

Rosa explains that people differ in when their clocks run, and that genes explain part of the difference. Larks wake early and feel best in the morning, owls come alive late at night, and most people lie in between.
Rosa's colleague Mina is a proud owl who works the late shift at the clinic. She laughs that she is useless before ten in the morning but brilliant at midnight.
The trouble comes when owls must start work or school early. They must wake at the wrong time for their clocks, which scientists call social jet lag.
Lena looks at her diary and realises that she is probably a mild owl. Even so, staying up until three is later than her clock needs, and the glowing phone is making it worse.
During puberty the body clock moves later, so teenagers feel sleepy at a later hour than children do. This shift is biological, and it can make waking for an early class feel like a fight.
Rosa says firmly that a teenager who struggles in the morning is not simply lazy. At seven in the morning the clock may still be telling the brain that it is the middle of the night.
Some schools have tried starting lessons later in the morning. In several studies the students slept more, and some schools reported that the students felt more alert.

The clock does not stop changing when we leave our teenage years, and it keeps moving as we age. Many older people feel sleepy earlier in the evening and wake earlier in the morning than they did when young.
Lena cannot change whether she is a lark or an owl, because that is partly in her genes. She can, however, nudge her clock with light, by getting bright light early and keeping the evenings dim.
Rosa draws a tower of small blocks, one for every hour that a person stays awake. Scientists link that pressure to a chemical called adenosine, which slowly builds up in the brain while we are awake.
Sleep clears the adenosine away again, which is why we wake up with the pressure low. The tower falls down, and a rested person starts the next day with a fresh pile of blocks.

At four in the morning an all-night student may suddenly feel better, because the body clock is pushing alertness upward. This second wind is a trick of the clock, and the tiredness comes back harder a little later.

Caffeine works by blocking the signal of adenosine, so the brain does not notice how tired it is. It hides the tiredness instead of removing it, and the tower of blocks is still growing behind the curtain.
Caffeine does not leave the body quickly, because about half of it is still there after five hours. The exact time differs from person to person, and it is longer for some than for others.
Lena counts the cups in her diary and finds that she drank six in one day. The last one was at nine in the evening, and she realises it was still in her body when she tried to sleep.
In one well-known experiment, volunteers drank coffee six hours before bedtime. Even then, their sleep was shorter than usual, although many of them said that they had not felt any effect.
Almost everyone feels a dip in alertness in the early afternoon. It is partly the body clock and not only lunch, so even people who skip the meal can feel the dip.

A short nap of about twenty minutes in the early afternoon can make a person feel sharper. A long nap late in the day is a different matter, because it uses up the sleep pressure that you need at night.
Lena tries a twenty-minute nap on the sofa, with Biscuit asleep on her feet. When the alarm rings she wakes up fresh, which has not happened to her for weeks.
Rosa tells Lena that sleep does not only rest the brain. It also helps the brain to store and organise what has been learned during the day.
Rosa compares the brain's short-term memory to a small inbox on a desk. Long-term memory is more like a library, and sleep helps to carry the important papers from the inbox to the shelves.
While we sleep, the brain seems to replay parts of the day in a kind of fast rehearsal. Brief bursts of brain activity during the lighter stages of sleep appear to help with this work.
In 1924 two researchers asked students to learn lists of meaningless syllables. Those who slept afterwards remembered more than those who stayed awake for the same number of hours.
Many later studies agree with that old experiment, and they have found the same pattern in different groups. Sleep after learning has been found to improve recall, from young children to adults.
The reverse seems to be true as well, and that matters to students. After a night without sleep the brain is worse at taking in new facts, a little like a sponge that is already full.
Lena closes her books at a sensible hour and makes a plan with Kofi. They will study in the day, sleep at night, and then repeat what they have learned the next morning.
Sleep does not help only with facts, but with skills too. In several studies, people who practised a task like typing a pattern or playing a piece of music did better after sleep.
Sleep may also help us to solve hard problems. In one study, people who slept after a puzzle were more likely to notice a hidden shortcut than people who stayed awake.
A few nights later Lena opens a practice paper and finds a question about a formula. To her surprise she remembers the formula that she had forgotten twice before.
Rosa tells Lena that the brain is only about two percent of the body's weight, but it uses a large share of its energy. All that work makes waste, and the brain has to clear it away somehow.

In mice, scientists found that the spaces between brain cells became wider during sleep. This let fluid wash through the brain more freely, a bit like a night cleaner who works when the offices are empty.
Rosa is careful to say that this finding comes mostly from animals. In people the evidence is still growing, and scientists do not yet know the whole story.
Some early studies suggest links between poor sleep and memory problems later in life. Rosa says this is an open question for science, and nobody should be frightened by it.
On the second day after a short night, a message from a friend annoys Lena far more than it should. Rosa nods, because poor sleep makes feelings stronger and people quicker to get irritated.

Brain scans have shown that a part of the brain which reacts to threats becomes more active after short sleep. At the same time the thinking part of the brain, which usually calms it, seems to have less control.
REM sleep may also help us to deal with feelings. One idea is that dreaming takes some of the sting from upsetting memories, although this has not been fully proved.
Rosa explains that sleep and mental health affect each other in both directions. Poor sleep can make a low mood worse, and a low mood can make it harder to sleep.
Rosa speaks gently, because Lena's friend Kofi has been feeling low for months. She says that a low mood which lasts is a good reason to see a doctor, and that she is not one herself.
After a few good nights Lena laughs more easily. Over lunch Kofi notices, and he asks her what her secret is.
Kofi arrives at Lena's flat sneezing through a heavy cold. Rosa tells them that sleep is one way the body supports its defences, which is why we often feel sleepy when we are ill.
In one study, researchers gave healthy volunteers a cold virus and watched who became ill. The people who had slept less in the days before were more likely to catch the cold.
Some studies also suggest that people who sleep well respond better to vaccines. Rosa says this research is still developing, but it shows how closely sleep and the body's defences are linked.
At night, blood pressure usually falls, which gives the heart and blood vessels a rest. Rosa says that this nightly dip is one of the quiet jobs that sleep does for us.
Large studies have linked long-term short sleep with higher blood pressure and heart problems. Rosa is careful to say that a link is not the same as proof, because many other factors play a part.
At two in the morning, Lena finds herself in front of the fridge, eating biscuits in the dim light. She wonders why she is hungry again, when she ate a big dinner only a few hours ago.

In experiments, short sleep seems to raise hormones that make us hungry and lower hormones that tell us we are full. Tired people often crave sweet and heavy foods, which may help to explain the biscuits.

In some studies, people who slept badly felt pain more strongly than people who slept well. Rosa says that poor sleep may turn up the volume on pain, and that people with pain should talk to a doctor.
After hard exercise the muscles need time to repair themselves, and sleep is part of that recovery. This is why many athletes treat sleep as part of their training and not as a break from it.
Rosa draws a house on a solid base and says that sleep is the base. It supports health, but it is not a cure-all, and anyone with a health worry should ask a doctor.
Rosa grows serious and tells them that driving while very tired is dangerous. Drowsy drivers cause many accidents, and the drivers often have no idea how close they are to sleep.
Rosa says that many people first come to her clinic after a near miss on the road. They fell asleep for a moment at the wheel, and they were frightened enough to ask for help.
