Body temperature follows the clock, falling through the evening to its lowest point in the early morning, and that dip is one of the signals that helps sleep to begin. It was an odd comfort to learn that the shiver she felt at four every morning was not a sign of weakness, only of the clock keeping time.

At six the next morning Rosa dragged her niece out into the park, where the grass was silver with dew and the first runners were already circling the lake. They passed in bright jackets, breathing steadily, some of them smiling with the air of people who had been born into a world designed for them. Lena yawned so widely that her jaw cracked, and she muttered that she did not belong in this world.

Rosa pointed to a runner and called him a lark, one of those people who wake early and feel at their best in the morning. Others are owls, who come alive late at night and fade at dawn, and many of the differences between them are written in their genes. Most people, she added, fall somewhere in the middle, and a person's type is not a moral quality but a feature of the clock.

Rosa's colleague Mina, who worked the late shift at the clinic, was a proud and unashamed owl. According to Rosa, Mina was completely useless before ten in the morning and quite brilliant after midnight, and the whole clinic had arranged itself around that fact. Her patients, who tended to be anxious at night, found her calm and cheerful, perhaps because she was at her very best at that hour.

The trouble starts, Rosa said, when an owl is forced to live by a lark's timetable. An owl who must be at a desk by eight, while his clock insists that it is still the middle of the night, lives in a state rather like permanent jet lag. Researchers even have a name for it, social jet lag, because he has travelled nowhere, yet his body behaves as if it had just crossed several time zones.

Lena studied her diary of the past few days with growing suspicion, and then with a small, embarrassed laugh. The evidence was plain: she was a mild owl who had pushed her natural tendency to an extreme by staying up until three with a bright phone in her hand. Being an owl, Rosa observed kindly, explains a late bedtime, but it does not explain a bedtime that has no end.

Then, Rosa said, there are teenagers, whose body clocks undergo a dramatic change at puberty. The clock shifts later, so that a fifteen-year-old may not feel sleepy until well after eleven, and may feel most alert in the evening. It is a biological shift and not a bad habit, and it explains why the same child who bounced out of bed at seven can seem impossible to wake a few years later.

Rosa was firm on one point: a teenager who struggles to get up for an early class is not simply lazy. At seven in the morning the clock of a sixteen-year-old may still be signalling the deepest part of the night, and no amount of shouting from the bottom of the stairs will change that. Lena remembered the teachers who had scolded her for yawning in class, and she felt, for the first time, a belated sympathy for her own teenage self.

Some schools have taken the evidence seriously and moved the start of the day later, and several studies of those changes have found that the students slept more. In some reports they also seemed more alert, although the results differ from place to place and the research is still going on. It is a hopeful sign that a problem which looks like a failure of character may sometimes be fixed with a change of timetable.

The clock does not stop changing when the teenage years end, Rosa said, and for older people it often moves in the opposite direction. Many older adults feel sleepy in the early evening and wake before dawn, and they often sleep more lightly than they did in youth. Lena thought of her grandmother, who sat by the window with a cup of tea at first light every morning, and finally understood why.

There was no way to turn an owl into a lark, Rosa said, because the type is partly built into the genes and the biology of the brain. But a clock can be nudged: bright light early in the day pulls it earlier, and dim, warm light in the evening lets it settle. Lena looked at her desk lamp, her ceiling light and her glowing phone, and realised that she had been shining a spotlight on the wrong half of the day.

Rosa drew a little tower made of building blocks, one block for every hour that a person stays awake. The longer you stay up, she said, the taller the tower grows, and scientists link this growing pressure to a chemical called adenosine, which slowly builds up in the brain through the waking hours. It is a bit like the pressure inside a bottle that is shaken again and again, and sooner or later it demands release.

Sleep, Rosa explained, is how the brain clears the adenosine away again, night after night, without any help from us. While we lie unconscious the tower is quietly dismantled, so that a rested person begins the next day with a small pile of blocks and a mind that feels light. The reverse is also true, and it is why a person who has been awake for twenty hours feels not merely tired but weighed down.

Lena had always noticed that around four in the morning she sometimes felt strangely better, as if her tiredness had been lifted away. Rosa said that the effect is a trick played by the clock, which pushes alertness upward as dawn approaches even when the body has not slept. The second wind is real, but it is a loan, and the sleepiness always returns afterwards with interest.

Caffeine, said Rosa, is the world's most popular drug, and it works by an elegant piece of deception. It blocks the places where adenosine would normally land, so the brain does not receive the message that the tower is getting tall, and the person feels awake even though the pressure is still building. Nothing has been solved, merely hidden, and when the caffeine wears off the whole load arrives at once.

Caffeine does not leave the body in a hurry, Rosa pointed out, because about half of it may still be there after five hours. The time varies a great deal between people, and it can be much longer in some, but the result is that an afternoon coffee is often still active at bedtime. Lena counted on her fingers and discovered, with some dismay, that her coffee at nine in the evening had been working against her at two.

Lena opened Rosa's notebook and counted six drinks on a single day, with the last one at nine at night. It was an uncomfortable discovery, like opening a bill that she had not been expecting. She had told herself that she needed all of that coffee to stay awake, but she had not noticed that the coffee was also helping to keep her awake long after she wanted to stop.

Rosa described an experiment in which volunteers drank coffee six hours before their normal bedtime and then slept in a laboratory. Even at that distance, the coffee made their sleep measurably shorter, although many of them said afterwards that they had not noticed any effect at all. The finding is a useful warning that feeling fine is not the same as sleeping well.

Almost everyone feels a dip in alertness in the early afternoon, Rosa said, and Lena was surprised to learn that it is not only the fault of lunch. Part of it belongs to the body clock, which has a built-in lull in the middle of the day, so that even a person who skips the meal will feel the dip. In many warm countries the afternoon rest is a long-established custom, and Rosa said it may be a sensible one.

A short nap, Rosa said, can work wonders if it is brief and early: twenty minutes or so, taken in the early afternoon, can leave a person feeling sharper and calmer. A long nap late in the day is another matter, because it uses up the sleep pressure that should be saved for the night, and it can leave the napper groggy. As with so many things in sleep, the timing matters as much as the amount.

Lena tried a twenty-minute nap on the sofa that afternoon, with a blanket over her knees and Biscuit asleep on her feet. When the alarm rang she sat up slowly, expecting to feel worse, but instead she felt fresh and oddly cheerful, with the fog gone from her mind. It was a small thing, but it was the first time in weeks that she had woken up and not wished to go straight back to sleep.

Rosa moved on to the subject that had brought Lena into this whole adventure: learning. Sleep does not merely rest the brain, she said, but helps it to store and organise everything it has taken in during the day. A student who gives up sleep to gain study time may therefore be throwing away the very thing that makes the study stick.

Rosa offered a comparison that Lena could hold in her head: the brain's short-term memory, she said, is like a small inbox on a desk, while long-term memory is like a vast library. During the day the inbox fills with new papers, and at night the papers are sorted, labelled and carried to the right shelves. If the sorting never happens, the inbox overflows, and the most recent papers are the first to slip off the desk.

While we sleep, Rosa explained, the brain appears to replay recent experiences in a kind of fast, quiet rehearsal, and this replay seems to strengthen the traces that matter. The brief bursts of activity called spindles, which appear in the lighter stages of sleep, seem to be involved, although scientists are still working out exactly how. What is clear is that the sleeping brain is not idle, but is doing the filing that the waking brain has no time to do.

One of the oldest experiments on the subject, she said, took place in 1924, when two researchers asked students to learn lists of meaningless syllables and tested them later. The students who slept in between remembered more than those who stayed awake for the same number of hours, and the difference was clear. It was a simple experiment, but it has been echoed by many more careful ones in the century since.

Later studies, Rosa went on, have found the same pattern in people of nearly every age, from small children learning new words to adults memorising facts. Sleep soon after learning generally gives better recall than staying awake for the same period, though the size of the effect varies from one task to another. Lena was struck by how reassuring it was to hear a result that did not depend on being young, clever or lucky.

The opposite also appears to be true, said Rosa, and it matters a great deal to students. After a night without sleep the brain is worse at taking in new information, as if the inbox had been stuffed so full that nothing more could be pushed in. Lena thought of the all-night sessions that had left her staring at a page without remembering a word, and wondered how many of those hours had been wasted from the start.

That afternoon Lena called Kofi, and together they made a plan that went against everything they had done so far. They would study during the day, close their books at a sensible hour, sleep through the night, and then spend ten minutes the next morning recalling what they had learned. Kofi grumbled that it sounded too easy to work, but he agreed to try it for a few days, if only to prove her wrong.

Sleep helps with skills as well as with facts, Rosa went on, and the evidence for this is quite strong. In a number of studies, people who practised a pattern of finger movements, like a short piece of piano music or a typing task, performed better after a night of sleep than after the same number of hours spent awake. It seems that the brain goes on practising while the body lies still, smoothing the rough places in a new skill.

Sleep may even help the brain to find solutions that it could not see before. In one well-known type of study, people were given a puzzle with a hidden shortcut, and those who had slept after working on it were more likely to spot the shortcut than those who had stayed awake. Rosa was careful to say that research on this is still developing, but she thought it a charming reminder of why people say that they will sleep on a problem.

A few days later, Lena opened a practice paper and found a question that depended on a formula she had stumbled over twice before. To her astonishment the formula came back to her whole, as if someone had quietly slipped it into her mind while she was not looking. She wrote it at the top of the page, and then she smiled, because she knew exactly where it had come from.

Rosa's next topic was the brain's night shift, and she began with a surprising fact about its appetite. The brain is only about two percent of the body's weight, yet it uses a far larger share of its energy, and all that busy work produces waste. Like any busy factory, she said, it has to find some way of clearing away the rubbish.

In mice, Rosa explained, scientists have seen that the spaces between brain cells grow wider during sleep, allowing fluid to flow through the brain more freely and carry waste away. Some researchers describe it as a kind of night cleaning crew that works while the offices are empty. It is an attractive picture, and Lena could not help imagining her own brain being gently washed while she slept.

Rosa raised a finger, because she wanted to be quite honest about how much is known. The finding comes largely from experiments on animals, she said, and in people the evidence is still growing, so it would be a mistake to treat the cleaning idea as settled fact. Good science, she added, is the habit of saying what we know and what we only suspect.

There are some early hints, Rosa said, that long-term poor sleep may be linked with memory problems in later life, and researchers are working hard to find out whether the link is real and which way it runs. At this stage it is an open question and not a warning, and nobody should lie awake at night worrying about it. Lena laughed, and said that would be a very silly way to lose sleep.

On the second morning after a short night Lena received a harmless message from a friend, and to her own surprise she felt a wave of irritation, quite out of proportion to anything the friend had said. Rosa nodded when she heard about it, because tired people tend to feel emotions more strongly and to lose their patience more quickly. It was a relief to discover that her bad temper had a reason, and that she was not simply turning into a worse person.

Brain scans, Rosa explained, have shown that a small region which responds to threats and strong feelings becomes more active after a short night. At the same time the thinking part of the brain, which normally helps to keep that alarm under control, seems to have a weaker grip on it. A tired person, in other words, has a louder alarm and a weaker hand on the volume switch.

Rosa added that REM sleep may have a part to play in the way we deal with our feelings, and she described one idea that scientists find attractive. During dreaming the brain may replay upsetting memories in a calm chemical setting, taking away some of the sting while keeping the memory itself. It is an idea and not a proven fact, she said, but it would explain why a problem often looks smaller in the morning.

Sleep and mental health, Rosa told her, push and pull on each other in both directions. Poor sleep can make a low mood worse, and a low mood can make it harder to sleep, so that a person can become caught in a loop in which each problem feeds the other. Understanding the loop, she said, is the first step toward asking for help in good time.

Rosa lowered her voice, because she knew that Kofi had been feeling very low for several months, and she wanted to be careful. If a low mood lasts for weeks, she said, it is a good reason to see a doctor, and sleep habits are no substitute for that advice. She reminded Lena that she was a sleep technician and not a doctor, and that the kindest thing a friend can do is to encourage someone to ask for proper help.

After a few good nights Lena found that her mind was lighter, and she caught herself laughing at a joke before the end of the punch line. Over lunch on Thursday Kofi noticed the change, and he looked at her across the table with an expression of suspicious curiosity. He asked what her secret was, and for the first time she answered without a trace of embarrassment that she had been going to bed.

On Monday Kofi arrived at Lena's flat sneezing through a heavy cold, and he collapsed onto the sofa with a box of tissues. Rosa, who happened to be visiting, told them that sleep is one of the ways in which the body keeps its defences in good repair. It is no accident, she said, that we feel so sleepy when we are ill, because the body is calling for the very thing that helps it to recover.

Rosa described a study in which healthy volunteers were deliberately exposed to a common cold virus and then watched carefully to see who became ill. The people who had slept less in the days before the exposure were more likely to catch the cold, although the researchers noted that many other things can also play a part. Kofi groaned that he had never thought of his three-hour nights as an invitation to the virus.

There is also some evidence, Rosa told them, that people who sleep well may respond better to certain vaccines, producing a stronger defence in the weeks that follow. The research is still developing, and the size of the effect is not yet clear, so she would not advise anyone to change a medical plan because of it. What it shows, she said, is how closely sleep and the body's defences are woven together.

The heart, Rosa said, also gets a rest at night, and that rest is built into the body's daily rhythm. In most healthy people, blood pressure falls while they sleep, giving the heart and blood vessels a quieter shift, and doctors sometimes worry when that nightly dip fails to appear. It is one of those silent jobs that sleep performs for us, and nobody ever thanks it.

Large studies, Rosa went on, have found that people who regularly sleep too little over many years are more likely to have high blood pressure and heart problems. She was careful to add that a link is not the same as proof, because people who sleep poorly may also differ in other ways, and scientists are still sorting out cause from coincidence. The honest message is that there is good reason to protect sleep, not that a few short nights will damage anyone's heart.

At two in the morning, a few nights earlier, Lena had found herself in front of the open fridge, eating biscuits in the dim yellow light and not even tasting them. She had told herself that she was hungry from studying, but she had eaten a large dinner only a few hours before. Rosa smiled when she heard the story, because she had a feeling that she knew the explanation.

In laboratory experiments, Rosa said, short sleep tends to raise a hormone that makes us feel hungry and to lower one that tells us we are full. Tired people also tend to crave sweet and heavy foods, and they may have less self-control when they meet them in the middle of the night. It was not a failure of will, then, but a signal from a tired body that wanted fuel, and the best answer was not to eat less but to sleep more.

Rosa mentioned that sleep and pain are also linked, and that in several studies people who slept badly felt pain more strongly than people who slept well. It may be that a tired nervous system turns up the volume on every signal, including the unpleasant ones. She was quick to add that pain which lasts should always be looked at by a doctor, and that nobody can sleep it away.

After hard exercise the muscles are slightly damaged and need time to repair, and sleep is an important part of that recovery. Rosa said that many athletes now treat sleep as part of their training, and that some teams have even tested whether more sleep improves performance. In small studies of this kind, athletes who slept longer sometimes did better, although the research is limited and the results vary.

Rosa took a pen and drew a small house standing on a wide, solid base, and she wrote the word sleep along the bottom. It supports everything above it, she said, but it is a foundation and not a cure-all, and nobody should expect good sleep to fix every problem. If you are worried about your health, she added firmly, the right person to ask is a doctor.

Rosa's face grew serious as she turned to the subject that frightened her most, which was driving while tired. A drowsy driver, she explained, is a real danger to everyone on the road, and drowsy driving is thought to contribute to a great many crashes every year. The most worrying thing is that people often have no idea how close they are to falling asleep until it is too late.

Many of the patients who came to her clinic, Rosa said, arrived there after a near miss on the road. They had closed their eyes for a moment at the wheel, and when they opened them again the car had drifted across the white line, and the shock was enough to make them ask for help at last. She said it with no drama at all, and Lena found that this made it more powerful.

Rosa told them about experiments in which volunteers were kept awake and then tested on tasks that resembled driving. After about seventeen hours without sleep, their performance was already affected in roughly the same way as it would be by a small amount of alcohol, and after a whole day and night awake the effect was far greater. Nobody, she said firmly, would hand the car keys to a person who had been drinking, and a person who has been awake all night deserves to be treated in the same way.

A microsleep, Rosa explained, is a brief intrusion of sleep into the waking day, lasting anywhere from a second or two to perhaps half a minute. It arrives without a warning, the eyes may even stay open, and the person often has no memory of it afterwards, which is exactly what makes it so dangerous. At a desk it is merely embarrassing, but at the wheel of a car it can be disastrous.

The next day, in a lecture hall, Lena felt her pen slide off the page and her head drop forward, and she jerked upright with her heart thumping. When she looked around, the lecturer had moved on to a new board, and a whole minute of the talk had vanished from her mind as if it had never been spoken. It was the first time she had ever seen a microsleep from the inside, and the experience was frightening in its smoothness.

The warning signs, Rosa said, are yawning again and again, heavy eyes, drifting in the lane, missing a turn or forgetting the last few kilometres. A driver who notices them should stop in a safe place and rest, perhaps with a short nap, because opening the window or turning up the radio does nothing to remove the cause. The one cure, she said, is sleep, and everything else is only a delay.

Kofi announced proudly that he coped perfectly well on five hours of sleep and had done so for years. Rosa answered patiently that in laboratory tests most people who make this claim still perform worse than when they are well rested, and that they are often the last to notice it. It is a curious feature of lost sleep, she said, that it damages the very faculty we would use to judge the damage.

A very small number of people, Rosa conceded, really do need less sleep than the rest of us, and scientists have traced the trait to rare changes in certain genes in a few families. These people are the exception that proves how difficult it is to be one, and wishing to belong to that group does not make it so. For nearly everyone, she said, the sensible assumption is that the usual numbers apply.

After a good night's sleep, Lena played Rosa's reaction game again, with her aunt watching over her shoulder and Kofi peering at the screen. This time her finger tapped faster and more steadily, and the score was so much better than before that she laughed out loud. It was a small proof, but it was her own, and it was far more convincing than anything she had been told.

Kofi watched the screen in silence, and for once he did not make a joke. Then he asked, in a rather small voice, whether Lena would mind lending him a notebook, because he wanted to see what his own numbers looked like. Rosa said nothing at all, but she smiled the smile of a teacher who has just seen the first hand go up.

Rosa introduced a new idea with the help of a bank, because she said that missing sleep is much like borrowing money. Every short night adds to a debt, and the body, like a patient lender, keeps careful track and expects to be repaid in the end. The trouble, she added, is that the interest tends to be paid in poor concentration, bad moods and a general sense of living at half speed.

On Saturday Lena slept until noon and woke feeling extremely pleased with herself, convinced that she had paid off her whole debt at a stroke. Rosa gently deflated her by explaining that a long sleep can repay part of the debt, but that studies suggest weekend lie-ins do not repair all of the damage, especially when the week has been full of short nights. It is better than nothing, she said, but it is not a miracle, and it cannot replace regular sleep.

A very late weekend also carries a price of its own, Rosa warned, because sleeping until noon moves the body clock later and leaves it out of step with Monday's early start. The result feels exactly like jet lag, though no plane has been boarded, and it can take days to put right. Lena groaned aloud, because she knew precisely what a Monday morning like that felt like.

The gentlest way to repay a debt, Rosa said, is to go to bed a little earlier for several nights in a row, adding perhaps half an hour or so each evening until the tiredness fades. This is easier on the body clock than a sudden marathon sleep, and it leaves the wake-up time as steady as before. Lena liked the sound of it, because it did not require any heroic effort, only a little patience.

Rosa told them that human beings are just one chapter in a very long book, and that animals sleep in wonderfully different ways. A cat may sleep for twelve to sixteen hours a day, which made Lena look at Biscuit with new respect, and some bats are said to sleep even longer, while wild elephants may manage with only a few hours. Every species has found its own answer to the question of how to sleep, and each answer fits the life it leads.

The most ingenious solution, Rosa said, belongs to the dolphin, which cannot afford to fall fully asleep, because it must rise to the surface every few minutes to breathe. Instead, it sleeps with one half of its brain at a time, so that one eye stays open, the body keeps gliding and the other half of the brain rests. Rosa said it was the nearest thing in nature to a night watchman who never leaves his post.

Some other animals also use half-sleep, Rosa went on, and scientists have observed it in certain birds and in seals. In one famous series of observations, birds sleeping at the edge of a group kept the eye that faced outward open, as if each one were standing guard for the others. Sleep, it seems, is always a bargain between rest and safety, and each creature settles the price in its own way.

On Tuesday morning Lena came to breakfast with a story about a dream in which she was running through a vast hall of desks, and every exam paper was written in a language that she had never seen before. She told it with great drama, and Rosa laughed until her tea shook in the cup. Lena had to admit, however, that waking up with the sun on her face and the exam still two weeks away was a great relief.

Rosa admitted that scientists do not yet fully understand why we dream, and she said that she preferred honesty to a neat answer. Some researchers believe that dreams help the brain to sort memories and to process emotions, while others suspect that they may be a by-product of a very busy brain, a kind of display on a screen. Whatever the truth, she said, the dream is a reminder that the sleeping brain is far from silent.

Everyone dreams, Rosa told them, even the people who insist that they never do, and the reason they forget is that dreams fade within minutes of waking unless we make an effort to hold them. Bad dreams are common and usually perfectly normal, though a doctor can help if they come very often or are very distressing. Lena found it strangely comforting that a strange dream about an exam in a foreign language was something that so many people shared.

Rosa walked through Lena's bedroom like an inspector arriving at a crime scene, and Lena followed her with growing embarrassment. There was a work desk pushed against the side of the bed, a bright lamp, a tangle of cables and a phone that glowed through the night like a small lighthouse. Rosa said nothing for a full minute, and then she remarked mildly that the room looked like an office with a mattress in it.

Darkness, Rosa told her, is one of the most important gifts a bedroom can give, because even small lights can reach the eyes through closed lids and tell the brain that it is not yet night. Lena bought thick curtains and a soft sleep mask, and she covered the little blinking lights on her charger with strips of tape. It looked a little silly, but when she turned off the lamp the room became truly dark for the first time in months.

Quiet matters too, Rosa said, though people differ greatly in how much noise they can ignore, and some sleep soundly through a thunderstorm while others wake at a dripping tap. Earplugs or a steady, gentle background sound can cover the sudden noises of the street, which are often more disturbing than constant ones. Lena had always assumed that she was used to the traffic, but she had never tested whether her sleeping brain agreed.

The body needs its temperature to fall in order to sleep, so a bedroom that is slightly cool tends to work best. Many experts suggest a temperature of around sixteen to eighteen degrees, with enough blankets to feel comfortable, although the right number varies from person to person. Lena, who had always kept her room as warm as a greenhouse, was surprised to find that she slept better with the window open a crack.

Rosa asked Lena to carry her desk out of the bedroom, and she explained why with a simple idea from psychology. When the bed is used only for sleep, the brain learns to link it with rest, whereas a bed that is also an office teaches the brain to expect work and worry. Lena dragged the desk into the corner of the living room, and the empty space in the bedroom felt calm and slightly surprising.

Rosa laughed when Lena asked her which mattress and pillow she should buy, and she said that there is no magic bed and no perfect pillow. The right bed is simply one that feels comfortable to the person who sleeps in it, and an expensive purchase will not repair a bad routine. Lena decided that her old mattress was not so bad after all, and she felt rather relieved to save the money.

Lena turned her alarm clock around so that it faced the wall and could not be seen from the pillow. Rosa explained that watching the minutes crawl by at night only increases anxiety, because it turns every wakeful moment into a small countdown to disaster. Worry, she said, is the great enemy of sleep, and a clock that cannot be seen cannot add to it.

An hour or two before bed, Rosa suggested, Lena might take a warm bath, and the advice seemed so pleasant that she hardly needed persuading. The body warms in the water and then cools afterwards, and that fall in temperature is itself a signal that helps sleep to begin. It is one of the few pieces of sleep advice, Rosa said with a smile, that can be followed with bubbles.

The first night in the changed bedroom felt strange to Lena, and she lay stiffly in the dark, listening to the silence. The room was cooler, the desk was gone and the phone was out of reach, and for a long time she wondered what on earth to do with her hands. Eventually the strangeness faded into drowsiness, and she fell asleep without noticing the exact moment.

The next morning Rosa warned her that the real benefits of such changes take days to show, and that she should be patient with herself. Lena did notice small signs, however, such as waking before the alarm and feeling a little less foggy over breakfast. It was not a miracle, but it was something, and she wrote it down in the notebook with a small, pleased flourish.

Rosa moved on to something that she called the problem of the midnight window, and she said it was the easiest of all sleep problems to fix. Bright light in the evening can delay sleepiness by holding back the signal that tells the body that night has arrived. Dim, warm light in the last hours of the day, she explained, is far kinder to the body clock.

For years Lena had scrolled through her phone in bed, as if it were a natural part of closing the day, and that night she caught herself still scrolling at two. She asked herself why she did not feel sleepy, given that she had been awake for twenty hours, and then she looked down at the glowing rectangle in her hand. The answer to her question, she began to suspect, was looking straight back at her from the glass, bright and patient and wide awake.

In one well-known study, volunteers who read from a light-emitting tablet before bed released melatonin later than those who read a paper book, and they took longer to fall asleep. They also felt less alert the following morning, even though they had slept for the same number of hours. Rosa said that this was one experiment among many, but that its message had been repeated often enough to be worth taking seriously.

Light, Rosa said, is not the whole story, because the content on the screen matters as well. Endless videos, news and messages keep the mind busy and slightly agitated, and a phone is built by clever people who want you to take one more look. A bright screen in a dark room is therefore a double problem, as it tells the eyes it is daytime and tells the mind there is more to see.

That afternoon Lena went to a shop and exchanged her bright white bulb for a soft yellow one, and she put a dim lamp in the corner of the living room. In the evening the flat looked like a quiet cafe, and she was surprised to find that she liked it far more than the hard glare she had lived with. Even Biscuit seemed to approve, because she stretched out under the lamp and began to purr.

Many phones have a night mode, Rosa said, which turns the colour of the screen warmer after sunset, and it is a sensible feature. It helps a little, but it does not solve the problem, because the content still tempts the mind, and the best solution is simply to put the phone away. Lena thought about this for a moment and admitted that it was the answer she had been trying to avoid.

Lena decided to charge her phone in the kitchen overnight, and she stood and looked at the cable on the counter as if she were signing a treaty. It was only ten steps from her bed, but she knew that those ten steps would be enough to stop her from reaching out in the dark. For the first time in years, she went to sleep without the cold blue light of the screen on her face.

Kofi was worried that he would miss important messages in the middle of the night, because his family lived in another time zone. Rosa suggested a silent mode that allowed only real emergencies to get through, and after a moment of doubt Kofi agreed to try it for a week. He admitted, a few days later, that nothing urgent had happened and that he felt oddly free.

Lena bought a cheap round alarm clock with a loud old-fashioned bell, and she placed it on the bedside table like a small trophy. The phone, after all, had been waking her for years, and every morning it had delivered an unwelcome parcel of notifications along with the alarm. With a simple clock beside her bed, the phone could stay in the kitchen and leave her mornings in peace.

The first hour without a phone was boring, and Lena kept reaching for a screen that was not there, like a person feeling for a missing tooth. By the third evening, however, she had taken a paper novel from the shelf and was reading it by a small lamp, with Biscuit curled up beside her. She was surprised to find that she was enjoying herself, and even more surprised to find that she was sleepy.

Rosa announced that the most powerful habit of all was also the least exciting, and it was a regular wake-up time. A body clock, she said, loves rhythm, and it learns from repetition when the day begins, even at weekends, so that waking and sleeping start to arrive at the same hour on their own. A fixed morning, in other words, is the anchor that holds the whole day in place.

Rosa did not ask for perfection, because she knew that real life is full of late parties and early trains. If the wake-up time stays within about an hour every day, she said, the clock has a steady anchor, and an occasional exception does little harm. Lena found the idea restful, since it asked only for rough consistency and not for iron discipline.

Every morning, now, Lena stood on the balcony with a cup of tea and let the light fall on her face, and she began to look forward to it. Bright morning light and a few minutes outdoors help the body clock to set itself for the day ahead, and the effect is stronger than almost any other habit. It was not just good for her sleep, she noticed, but it made the whole morning feel as if it belonged to her.

Rosa pointed to the grey sky above the rooftops and said that it was still far brighter out there than inside any ordinary room. Even on a cloudy day, the light outdoors can be many times stronger than the light indoors, and the clock responds to that difference. A person who spends the whole day inside, she added, may live in a kind of permanent dusk, however many lamps are lit.

For years Lena's finger had hovered over the snooze button every morning, like a diver about to step off a board. Rosa explained that snoozing mostly gives broken and shallow sleep, which does little good, and it can make the waking-up harder. Lena set a single alarm, placed the clock across the room and discovered that getting up at the first bell was a good deal easier than she had feared.

Rosa told her that feeling groggy for the first few minutes after waking is perfectly normal, and she gave the feeling its scientific name, sleep inertia. The brain does not switch on like a light, she said, but warms up like an engine on a cold day, and the grogginess usually fades within a short time without any help. Lena had always taken that heaviness as proof that she needed more sleep, and she was relieved to hear it was nothing of the kind.

To help herself wake up gently, Lena began a small morning routine: a glass of water, an open window and a few slow stretches by the bed. These little steps, she found, told her body that the day had begun, and the fog lifted far faster than it ever had when she lay there with her eyes closed. It was a modest ritual, but it made the first minutes of the day feel like a beginning and not like a battle.

Rosa returned to the subject of caffeine, because she wanted to give Lena a rule that she could live with. Many experts suggest limiting it in the afternoon and evening, since it stays in the body for hours, and a common guide is to stop at least six hours before bedtime, and earlier for people who are sensitive to it. Individual differences are large, she added, so the best test is to observe what happens to your own sleep.

Caffeine hides in more places than most people imagine, Rosa said, and the coffee cup is only the most obvious one. Tea, cola, energy drinks and even dark chocolate all contain some, and Kofi, who had been counting only his coffee, went rather pale when she listed the energy drinks. Lena began to read the labels on everything she bought, and she was amused to find how many of them carried a small, unwelcome surprise.

At four o'clock that afternoon Lena felt the familiar pull toward the coffee machine, and instead she poured herself a glass of water and walked once around the block. At first she missed the coffee badly, and her hand kept drifting toward the kettle, but the fresh air woke her up in a different and gentler way. When she came back, she felt that she had won a small argument with an old habit.

On Saturday evening Kofi held his birthday party, and his small flat overflowed with friends, music and an enormous chocolate cake. Someone pressed a glass of wine into Lena's hand, and she stood there for a moment with a feeling that she was being tested. Rosa had talked about alcohol earlier that week, and Lena found that she remembered every word.

Alcohol, Rosa had explained, is a clever impostor, because it can make a person feel drowsy at first and so it looks like a sleep aid. Later in the night, however, it breaks up sleep, causing frequent wakings that the sleeper may not remember, and it reduces REM sleep. A person who drinks to fall asleep is therefore buying a quick start at the cost of a poor night.

After drinking, Rosa continued, the first hours of the night may be deep, but the second half is usually lighter, more broken and less restful, so that the sleeper wakes in the morning feeling dull. Alcohol can also relax the muscles of the throat and make snoring and breathing problems worse. Lena looked at the glass, took a small sip, and quietly decided that one would be quite enough for the evening.

Rosa also warned about the evening meal, because a large, heavy dinner close to bedtime can disturb sleep while the body is still busy with digestion. A light snack is perfectly fine, she said, and nobody should go to bed with a growling stomach, since hunger can keep a person awake just as well as a feast. The secret, as in so many things, lies in moderation and in timing, and a little care with both goes a long way.

Lena asked about warm milk, which her grandmother had always given her before bed, and Rosa answered with her usual honesty. There is little strong evidence that milk itself helps, she said, but a quiet, cosy ritual can calm the mind, and that is no small thing. If a warm drink makes you feel safe and sleepy, then it is doing its job, whatever the chemistry.

Exercise, Rosa told her, is among the most reliable friends of sleep, and people who are regularly active tend to fall asleep faster and to sleep more deeply. For most people the time of day matters much less than the regularity, so the best exercise is the kind that one will actually do. It was a refreshing relief to hear advice that asked her to do something enjoyable, instead of giving something up.

On Sunday afternoon Lena put on her running shoes and jogged through the park beside Rosa, who ran with the calm rhythm of a person who had been doing it for years. The sun was low and golden, the leaves were scattered across the path, and for the first time in weeks Lena felt strong in her own body. By the second lap she had stopped thinking about her exam and was thinking only about her breathing.

Rosa added a small warning: very hard exercise close to bedtime may keep some people awake, because it raises the heart rate and the body temperature. She said that the effect varies, and that many people sleep well after an evening workout, so the best advice is to listen to your own body. Lena, who had no intention of sprinting at midnight, found it easy to agree.

There was another benefit, Rosa pointed out, in exercising outdoors in daylight, because it delivers two gifts at once. The body gets the movement that it needs, and the eyes get the bright light that helps to set the clock, so that sleep is helped from two sides at the same time. Lena thought it the most efficient bargain she had ever been offered, and she felt almost guilty for enjoying it so much.

By the end of the week Lena noticed something that made her sit up in bed with surprise: she was falling asleep within about ten minutes, instead of the hour or more that she had grown used to. She wrote the figure in her notebook and underlined it twice, because it seemed to her to be the first real proof that the plan was working. She did not yet know whether her exam would be easier, but she knew that her nights already were.

Rosa smiled and said that sleep is rather like a shy cat, because it cannot be forced and will only come when it is invited. The best invitation, she said, is a calm evening that slowly prepares the body and the mind, and the preparation begins an hour or two before the lights go out. Lena, who had always tried to command sleep like a general giving orders, saw at once why her campaigns had failed.

The first step, Rosa suggested, was a simple routine that Lena would repeat every night: dimming the lights, brushing her teeth, laying out her clothes and reading for a while. When the same steps happen in the same order, the body begins to recognise them as a signal, and sleepiness gathers almost by habit. It is the way that children are taught to sleep, she added, and the lesson works just as well for grown-ups.

Rosa described a small study in which people who spent five minutes writing a to-do list before bed fell asleep faster than people who wrote about things they had already done. She admitted that this was only one study, and that it should not be treated as a rule, but she thought that the idea made sense. A mind that is trying to remember tomorrow's tasks cannot easily let go of them, whereas a page can hold them safely.

That evening Lena wrote down the jobs for tomorrow, and then she added the worries that had been circling in her head like moths around a lamp. Seeing them on paper made them seem smaller and more manageable, and she closed the notebook with a feeling of relief that surprised her. She had expected the list to make her more anxious, but it was as if she had handed her worries to someone else for the night.

Rosa taught her a simple technique that she had learned at the clinic, in which the breath out is a little longer than the breath in. She also showed Lena how to relax the muscles one group at a time, starting with her toes and working upward until even her forehead was soft. Neither trick was magical, she said, but both gave the mind something quiet to do while the body slipped toward sleep.

A warm shower can be a lovely part of the wind-down, Rosa said, provided that the bathroom light is soft and the evening is not rushed. Lena tried it that night, and she enjoyed the warmth of the water, and afterwards she felt her body cool in the bedroom and begin to grow heavy. It was a small luxury, but it had the sort of effect that no pill could give her, because it came with a story and a rhythm.

One night Lena woke in the dark, and out of habit she turned toward the clock, but it faced the wall and she saw only its blank back. Rosa had told her that watching the time only raises worry, because every minute becomes a small accusation, so she let the thought go and closed her eyes again. After a few slow breaths, the time no longer seemed to matter at all.

Rosa explained that lying awake for a long time in bed can teach the brain to associate the bed with frustration and not with rest. If you cannot sleep for a good while, she said, the best plan is to get up and do something calm in dim light, such as reading a few pages, until you feel sleepy again. The point is not to punish yourself, but to protect the bed's reputation as a place where sleep happens.

At two in the morning Lena woke and could not return to sleep, so she followed Rosa's advice and padded into the living room with a paperback and a small lamp. She read a few pages by the soft light, with Biscuit watching her from the sofa, and after a short while her eyes began to feel heavy. She went back to bed, and she was asleep within minutes, which would have seemed impossible a week earlier.

Rosa and Lena sat in the quiet kitchen with their cups, and Rosa said something that Lena wrote down because she liked it so much. Sleep should never become a performance, she said, because trying too hard makes the body more awake and not less, and the harder you chase it, the faster it runs away. The best you can do is to prepare well, lie down gently and let the night do the rest.

Rosa turned to a subject that she described as the most common sleep complaint in the world, and that was insomnia. It means having trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early, and it is so widespread that nearly everyone will meet it at some point in life. Many people have a short spell of it during a stressful time and then recover, and that is not a cause for alarm.

Doctors reserve the word chronic for the kind of insomnia that lasts, Rosa explained, and the definition is quite precise. Chronic insomnia usually means that a person has had trouble sleeping at least three nights a week for about three months, together with tiredness or poor concentration in the daytime. A few bad nights, however upsetting, do not count, and Rosa said that this distinction is a comfort to many people who worry that they are ill.

Insomnia has many causes, said Rosa, and it would be a mistake to blame worry for all of them. Pain, noise, certain medicines, irregular habits and other health problems can all play a part, which is why a doctor must look carefully at the circumstances of each person. This is exactly the sort of case, she said, where general information is only a beginning and a personal conversation with a professional must follow.

For long-term insomnia, many medical guidelines now recommend a talking therapy as the first treatment, and not a pill. It is usually called cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, and it has good results for many people, often lasting longer than the effect of medicine. Lena was struck by the thought that the first treatment for a sleeping problem should be a conversation, but Rosa said that it made perfect sense.

The therapy teaches new sleep habits, Rosa said, such as keeping regular times and getting out of bed when you cannot sleep, and it also helps people to challenge the anxious thoughts about sleep that make the problem worse. A person who lies in bed thinking that tomorrow will be ruined is adding fuel to the fire, whereas a person who can speak to those thoughts calmly is quietly putting it out. A trained therapist can guide the process, she added, and it is not something to try alone with a book.

Sedative medicines, Rosa said, are a different matter altogether, and she chose her words with deliberate care. They can help some people for a short time, but they can also have side effects, and generally they are not the first answer to a long-term problem. They should be taken only when a doctor has decided that they are right, and nothing she said, she added, was meant as advice for any one person.

Kofi was quiet for a moment, and then he said that his uncle had not slept well for months and that the whole family was worried about him. Rosa answered gently that the kindest and most useful thing Kofi could do was to encourage his uncle to speak to his doctor, because a doctor can look for causes and offer proper help. Kofi nodded slowly and wrote himself a note on the back of his hand.

If poor sleep lasts for weeks, Rosa said, or if it begins to spoil the days, then the time has come to see a doctor, and there is no need to feel foolish about it. A doctor can ask the right questions, look for causes that nobody else would think of, and suggest treatments that fit the person, and the visit may be the start of a very different year. Waiting for the problem to disappear on its own is understandable, but it is seldom the quickest way.

Lena sat for a while looking out of the window at the grey morning, thinking about the many times she had called herself weak or lazy for being unable to sleep. She understood now that sleep problems are common and have many causes, and that asking for help is not weakness but the sensible thing to do. It was a gentle change of mind, and it felt like putting down a bag that she had carried for years.

Rosa said that Lena had learned a good deal about sleep in conversation, but that she had not yet seen how sleep is measured, and she thought it was time. She invited her to visit the clinic one evening and meet Mina, and see the machines and the quiet rooms where the work was done. Lena, who had never seen the inside of a sleep clinic, accepted at once, with a curiosity that had replaced her original scepticism.

Lena arrived at the clinic one evening expecting something like a hospital, with long white corridors and the smell of disinfectant. Instead she found a quiet building with soft lamps, where the bedrooms looked like small hotel rooms with wide beds, thick curtains and a bedside table. It was only the wires on the walls and the camera in the corner that told her that these were rooms where sleep was studied, and not simply enjoyed.

Mina, who was just beginning her night shift with a cup of tea and a contented yawn, showed Lena the sensors that she used. They were small discs that stick to the head, the face and the chest, recording the brain waves, the movements of the eyes, the activity of the muscles and the rhythm of the heart. Together they build a detailed map of an entire night, said Mina, and the word for the whole procedure is polysomnography, which she said she still could not pronounce when she was tired.

There were also a soft belt for the chest, a small clip for a finger and a thin tube that rests below the nose. These devices measure the movement of the breath and the amount of oxygen in the blood, and they help the staff to spot problems that happen only during sleep. Lena held one of the clips on her fingertip, and it glowed a gentle red, like a very small lighthouse.

Mina went on to explain one of the most important problems that the clinic sees, which is called sleep apnoea. In this condition, breathing stops or becomes very shallow many times during the night, sometimes for ten seconds or more, and the sleeper may have no idea that it is happening. It is one reason why some people can sleep for eight hours and still wake up exhausted.

In the most common kind of apnoea, Mina explained, the muscles of the throat relax so much during sleep that the airway narrows or closes. Each time this happens, the brain briefly wakes the sleeper just enough to restart the breathing, usually without any memory of it, and the cycle can be repeated many times in an hour. The sleeper does not remember a single one of these awakenings, but the night has been cut into pieces.

Mina listed the warning signs for Lena: loud snoring, gasping or choking in the night, stopped breathing noticed by a partner, morning headaches and heavy tiredness during the day. Anyone who notices them, she said, should talk to a doctor, because the condition is common and treatable, and the sooner it is found, the better. She said this calmly and without any alarm, as someone who had said it a thousand times before.

Many people do not know that they have apnoea, Mina said, because they are asleep when it happens, and it is often a partner who notices the snoring and the long silences. A sleep study at a clinic can measure it, and a doctor can then decide what to do next. Lena thought of the sleeping stranger in the next room, who had come to the clinic for this very reason, and she felt a quiet respect for his courage.

Treatments exist, Mina said, and a doctor chooses which of them is right for each person, because no single answer suits everyone. Some people use a small mask that gently keeps the airway open with a stream of air, while others change certain habits or use other methods, and each plan is made by the doctor and the patient together. Lena found it reassuring that a problem so alarming to describe could be treated so quietly.

From a small control room, Lena watched a screen on which the night of a sleeping volunteer was drawn as a long, rolling line. She recognised the slow, towering waves of deep sleep, the brief spindles of the middle stage and the busy, jagged trace of dreaming, and she felt a flush of pride in knowing what she was seeing. Only a few weeks earlier, it would have looked to her like nothing but a tangle of scribbles.

Lena walked home along the quiet streets as dawn began to colour the sky, with the lamps still lit and the first bakery opening its doors. She thought about all the hidden work that goes on inside every sleeping person, night after night, and she was astonished that she had spent so many years ignoring it. For the first time she felt that sleep was not a gap in her life, but a part of it, and one of the best.

On Wednesday Kofi arrived at Lena's flat with a wristband that gave him a sleep score every morning, and he displayed it to her with immense pride. The screen was full of coloured graphs, wavy lines and a large number out of one hundred, which he treated rather like a school report. Lena admired it politely, but she suspected that the number had been making him quite anxious.

Rosa explained how such trackers work, and she was neither harsh nor naive about them. They estimate sleep from the movement of the wrist and the rhythm of the heart, she said, which makes them reasonably good at telling you roughly when you slept and for how long, but only approximate at identifying the stages. Without a clinic's sensors, there is no way to see the brain waves directly, so any claim about deep sleep should be taken with a pinch of salt.

Rosa warned that too much attention to the numbers can itself cause trouble, and that some people actually sleep worse because they begin to worry about their scores. There is even a name for the habit of becoming obsessed with perfect sleep data, orthosomnia, which sounds like a disease but is really a state of mind. A tracker, Rosa said, should be a mirror in which you look now and then, and never a judge that you must please.

Kofi asked about sleeping pills and the supplements that he had seen in advertisements, and Rosa chose her words carefully, as she always did when the subject turned to medicine. They should be discussed with a doctor or a pharmacist, she said, because what suits one person may be unsuitable for another, and she was in no position to recommend anything. She reminded them that this book of facts was only general information, and not a substitute for personal advice.

Melatonin, Rosa said, is a good example of how confusing the rules can be, since it is sold in different ways in different countries. In some places it requires a prescription, while in others it is sold freely on the shelf, and the quality and the strength of products may vary from one brand to the next. A pharmacist is the right person to ask, she said, and a doctor if there is any doubt.

Rosa told them about jet lag, which happens when the body clock is still running on the old time after a long flight, so that the traveller feels sleepy at noon and wide awake at midnight. The clock adjusts only by about an hour a day, she said, and the timing of light can help to speed the change, though the best timing depends on the direction of travel. Lena promised herself that if she ever flew to another continent, she would remember this conversation.

Mina works through the night, so Rosa spoke next about shift work, which she called one of the great challenges of modern sleep. Night shifts force the body to work when the clock expects rest and to rest when the clock expects activity, and in the long run that can take a toll on health. Good light at work, a dark and quiet bedroom for the daytime sleep and a regular pattern can all reduce the strain, and Mina swears that her blackout curtains are her best friends.

Rosa laughed as she remembered her sister's baby, who had slept in short pieces of two or three hours and had made the whole household into a team of weary soldiers. Newborn sleep is simply like that, she said, because tiny babies have short cycles and need frequent feeding, and tired new parents are completely normal. They deserve patience, practical help and a good deal of sympathy, and Lena resolved to remember it the next time a friend became a parent.

Lena's grandmother, who lived nearby, had told her proudly that she hardly slept at all any more, and Lena now asked Rosa whether that was possible. Rosa answered that older people often sleep more lightly and wake more often, but that their need for sleep does not simply vanish, and a doctor can help if the problem is troubling them. Lena decided to visit her grandmother on Sunday and to ask, kindly, how she was really sleeping.

After dinner Rosa produced a quiz with five common sleep myths, and she read them aloud with the air of a game-show host. Lena and Kofi looked at one another over the table and took turns to guess, and one by one they discovered that every myth was wrong. The myths were that you can train yourself to need less sleep, that snoring is harmless, that wine helps, that the brain switches off and that a recording can teach a language overnight.

On the night before the exam, Lena felt the old temptation to read one more chapter, one more page, one more set of notes. She looked at the clock, which said ten, and for a moment the thought of the two weeks behind her wavered like a candle in a draught. Then she closed her books with a firm little click, because she now knew that the night ahead would do more for her than another hour at the desk.

Lena followed her entire routine without hurrying: a dim lamp, a warm shower, a short list of tomorrow's jobs and the phone left on the kitchen counter. The bedroom was dark and cool, the clock faced the wall, and Biscuit settled on her feet and began to purr like a tiny engine. Within a few minutes she was asleep, and for once there was no battle to fight.

For two weeks she had followed the plan, and now she woke a few minutes before her alarm, with the room full of pale gold light and her mind unusually quiet. She lay still for a moment, listening to the traffic far below, and realised that she felt calmer and clearer than she had for months. It was a strange sensation, she thought, to feel rested on the very morning when she had expected to feel afraid.

She allowed herself a few minutes on the balcony with a cup of tea, and she let the morning light fall on her face while the city below began to wake. Then she ate a light breakfast, drank a glass of water, packed her pens and checked her bag one last time, exactly as Rosa had suggested. It was an ordinary routine, but it felt like a ceremony, and she performed it with a quiet kind of pride.

Kofi was waiting outside the exam hall, and to her surprise he looked almost cheerful, with none of the grey exhaustion that she had seen on his face a fortnight earlier. He had followed the plan for the whole of the last week, he said, and it was the first time in his life that he had not felt panic before an examination. They walked in together, side by side, like two soldiers who had finally been properly fed and rested.

In the hall Lena took her seat and looked around at the other students, many of whom looked grey and hollow-eyed, clutching coffee cups and last-minute notes. She felt entirely different: alert but unhurried, with a clear head and steady hands, and no sense of the usual flutter in her stomach. The clock on the wall ticked quietly, and when the invigilator said that they might begin, she turned over the paper with a small, calm smile.

On the second page there was a question that made Lena's heart jump, because it asked about something that she had barely glanced at. For a moment she felt the old panic rise like a tide, and then she took a slow breath, as she had practised at night, and waited. One by one the facts came back to her, as if someone had quietly filed them away overnight and left a neat label on every drawer.

When the exam ended, Lena walked out of the hall into bright sunshine, feeling tired in a healthy way, the way a person feels after a long walk. She did not yet know what her result would be, and she was content not to know, because she was sure that she had given the paper her best. Kofi found her at the gate, and they stood together for a while, saying nothing, enjoying the warmth.

That evening Lena, Rosa and Kofi sat together on the balcony as the sky turned pink and then violet, with warm drinks in their hands and Biscuit asleep on a cushion nearby. Rosa said that she would not call sleep a kind of magic, because that would be unscientific, but she was proud that Lena had learned to give it a real place in her life. Lena lifted her cup and said that the experiment had worked, and that she would now keep the habit for good.

As evening settled over the city, Rosa and Lena drank warm milk on the balcony and agreed that sleep is no kind of magic, but that it quietly supports memory, mood, health and energy. This book has offered only general information, and it is not medical advice, so it cannot replace a conversation with a doctor who knows your own situation. If you are worried about your sleep, your tiredness or your health, please speak to a medical professional, and then go to bed on time.
